title: Project deep-dive structure, honest ownership, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs
objectives: Structure a Salesforce project deep-dive: context, your ownership, decisions, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs.
Use honest ownership: say what you did, what the team did, and what you would not claim.
Prefer measurable outcomes over adjective-only success, without inventing metrics you cannot defend.
Name a real trade-off (declarative vs Apex, build vs buy, sharing vs convenience) and a lesson that changed later work.
diagnostic_question: Tell me about a Salesforce project you led. How will you structure the answer so ownership, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs are audible in eight minutes?
definition: A project deep-dive is a structured story of one Salesforce delivery: context, honest ownership, decisions, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs. Trailhead career guidance tells you to highlight accomplishments with outcomes, use action verbs, and be accurate—do not lie or omit dates. Well-Architected gives language for the trade-offs you actually made (Trusted, Easy, Adaptable). ([Land your next opportunity](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/career-development-planning/land-your-next-opportunity); [Resume Writing Strategies](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/resume-strategies); [Well-Architected](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/overview))
why_it_matters: Deep-dives are where unverifiable hero stories die. Interviewers ask who wrote the trigger, what moved in a report, and what you would do differently. A structure keeps you from rambling; honesty keeps you from CAREER-009 failures.
sixty_second_explanation: Treat the deep-dive like an expedition after-action report. You do not claim you carried every pack. You show the map (context), who carried what (ownership), the GPS track (metrics), the fork in the trail (trade-offs), and what you would pack differently next time (lessons). Adjective-only 'it was a success' is a postcard with no coordinates.
deeper_explanation: Trailhead's landing-the-job unit contrasts action-verb accomplishments ('Designed an automated lead qualification process using Salesforce that resulted in XYZ') with vague duty lines ('Automated processes using Salesforce') and forbids lying. Deep-dives are spoken resumes with more room for trade-offs. ([Land your next opportunity](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/career-development-planning/land-your-next-opportunity))

Resume Writing Strategies lists work experience as a must-have and tells you to match the job description with skills you can demonstrate. A deep-dive should trace to a resume line you could defend. ([Resume plan](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/resume-strategies/resume-plan))

Career Development Planning uses a Discover/Plan/Act loop and a V2MOM-like worksheet for goals. A project story should still name a goal, measures, and obstacles. ([Create a plan](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/career-development-planning/create-a-plan-and-skill-up); [Assess yourself](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/career-development-planning/assess-yourself))

Well-Architected is the vocabulary for trade-offs: you chose Easy/readable Flow over clever Apex, or Trusted sharing over a convenient public field. ([Well-Architected](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/overview))

Interview Strategies reminds you to practice the story. Deep-dives are a story type, not a dump of every ticket. ([Interview Strategies](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/interview-strategies))

mental_model.analogy: Expedition after-action report: map, who carried which pack, GPS track, forks in the trail, what you would pack differently—not a postcard that says 'success.'
useful_mapping: honest ownership → who carried which pack
lessons → what you would pack next time
trade-offs → the pass you skipped to make camp
adjective-only success → a postcard with no coordinates
where_it_breaks: You may not have GPS (metrics). Say so; do not invent elevation.
Consulting engagements have client-owned packs; still name your pack.
This is not a military AAR product in Salesforce.
A 45-minute deep-dive is not a full program retrospective.

teach_back_prompt: Give an eight-minute deep-dive on one Salesforce project. Pause after ownership, after one metric, after one lesson, after one trade-off.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory, restate the core terms and one clarifying question you would ask.
Classify four realistic interview signals using this topic's decision table.
Teach the analogy, then name two places it breaks.
Walk one troubleshooting symptom from evidence to next action.
Give a two-minute interview answer without notes, then one follow-up.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: I structure a deep-dive as context, honest ownership, decisions, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs. I will not claim my teammate's Apex. If I lack a metric, I say so instead of inventing one.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I pick one slice I can defend, matching a resume line. I say the business problem and users. I name my pack versus the team's. I describe one which-tool or sharing decision. I give a before/after number only if I can name the report. I close with a lesson that changed later work and a trade-off in Trusted/Easy terms. I practice this story per Interview Strategies.

terminology.plain: A timed, structured story of one delivery.
terminology.precise: Context, ownership, decisions, metrics, lessons, trade-offs—practiced, not a ticket dump.
terminology.example: Eight minutes on a legal-freeze release you configured and tested.
terminology.non_example: Forty minutes listing every object in a three-year program you watched.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: STAR: a behavioral template (CAREER-008); deep-dive is the project-shaped version.
terminology.boundary: Pick a slice with a beginning and an end.

terminology.precise: Trailhead accuracy: do not lie. Say who wrote the trigger, who owned UAT, who was the vendor.
terminology.example: I built the validation rule and UAT cases; a developer wrote the callout.
terminology.non_example: We transformed the enterprise with no names.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: RACI: related FOUND-006 language you can reuse.
terminology.boundary: Consulting: the client still owned the org.

terminology.plain: A number or observable with a source.
terminology.precise: Before/after from a report, ticket count, UAT pass rate—or explicitly unknown.
terminology.example: Closed Won reversals after legal miss dropped from 6/quarter to 0 in two quarters, per LAB_ report.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: KPI: a business term; still needs a source.
terminology.boundary: Never invent. Inventing is a CAREER-009 fail.

terminology.plain: A change in your later practice.
terminology.precise: Not 'the business was hard.' A pack you would carry differently.
terminology.example: I now ask sharing questions before adding fields, after a legal comment leak scare.
terminology.non_example: Lessons learned: communicate more—without an example.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Blameless retro: a team ritual; still name your change.

terminology.plain: The option you did not take, and why.
terminology.precise: Well-Architected: Trusted versus Easy, readable Flow versus Apex service, buy versus thin build.
terminology.example: Chose a validation freeze instead of a legal AppExchange product this quarter.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Constraint: a given you could not change (license, deadline).
terminology.boundary: If you cannot name an alternative, the story sounds naïve.

terminology.plain: Problem, users, org constraints, time box.
terminology.precise: The map: what was broken for whom, in what Salesforce landscape.
terminology.example: Sales ops could not stop unreviewed Closed Won in Enterprise Edition, eight weeks to UAT.
terminology.non_example: Once upon a time we used Salesforce.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Scope: what was in and out, cousin of context.
terminology.boundary: Do not spend five minutes on company history.

terminology.plain: A fork you can still defend.
terminology.precise: Tool, sharing, SoR, or sequencing choice with a because.
terminology.example: Private child object instead of a public Opportunity field.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Accident: something that happened without a choice; say that too if true.
terminology.boundary: Tie decisions to CAREER-001 clarifying questions when relevant.

terminology.plain: The part of a program you actually owned.
terminology.precise: Deep-dives fail when you narrate a program. Shrink until ownership is honest.
terminology.example: The legal-freeze MVP, not the three-year CLM program.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Epic: agile term for a larger theme.
terminology.boundary: Interviewers prefer a sharp slice with metrics over a foggy program.

mechanics.observe: Interviewer can repeat who did what

mechanics.after: Forks, numbers or unknown, alternative not taken

A later project that used the lesson

when_to_use: When an interviewer asks for a Salesforce project deep-dive with ownership, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs.
When your resume line is thinner than the program and you must shrink to an honest slice.
When you are tempted to invent a metric rather than say unknown.
When you need Well-Architected language to name a real Trusted versus Easy choice.
When practicing a story per Interview Strategies so the eight minutes do not ramble.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a program-sized deep-dive when you only owned a validation rule.
Do not invent metrics, headcount, or savings you cannot source.
Do not claim Apex you did not write.
Do not skip trade-offs and lessons because the project 'went fine.'
Do not disclose confidential customer metrics or named clients if your NDA forbids it—use LAB_ labels.
configuration_or_code_location: Spoken story plus a one-page spine in notes
Resume line this story traces to
Optional sandbox screenshots of LAB_ reports, not customer orgs

worked_example.scenario: Interview: 'Walk me through a project you are proud of.' Your resume says 'Legal review on Opportunities.' The real program included a vendor CLM. You configured the freeze and UAT; a developer did the callout. You must show project deep-dive structure, honest ownership, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs.
inputs: You do not have a dollar savings number
You do have a reversal-count from a report you built

decisions.decision: Slice to the freeze MVP, not the CLM program. Name the developer's callout as theirs.
decisions.because: Honest ownership. Program fog would fail CAREER-009 later.
decisions.rejected: I led the enterprise CLM transformation

decisions.decision: Cite reversals 6→0 over two quarters from a report; trade-off = no AppExchange legal product; lesson = ask sharing first.
decisions.because: Metric has a source; trade-off is real; lesson changed later work.

configuration_or_code: Spine: context (unreviewed Closed Won), ownership (validation + UAT), decision (private child vs public field), metric (report), lesson (sharing questions), trade-off (thin freeze vs package).
worked_example.output: An eight-minute story the interviewer can audit against the resume.
verification: A peer can state what you personally did.
worked_example.self_explanation: After-action report with packs labeled; no postcard success.

hands_on_lab.environment: Notes app. Optional Trailhead profile for dates of badges, not as fake project proof.
starting_state_checks: You have one resume bullet about Salesforce work or a playground project
steps: Write the six headings: context, ownership, decisions, metrics, lessons, trade-offs.
Fill ownership with I/we/they in three bullets.
Fill metrics with a sourced number or the word unknown.
Write one alternative you did not take.
Write one lesson that changed a later decision.
Time a rehearsal at eight minutes; cut company history.
guided_completion: Highlight any sentence that claims others' work
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Rehearse a version for a business audience and a technical audience (CAREER-002) without changing ownership facts.

hands_on_lab.limitations: If you have no work history, use a playground project and say so honestly.

decision_table.signal: You supported a program but only owned UAT cases

decision_table.not: Narrate the whole program as yours
decision_table.why: Trailhead accuracy: do not lie; honest ownership is audible

decision_table.signal: You lack a dollar savings metric
decision_table.choose: Cite a report you have or say unknown; offer a qualitative UAT check

decision_table.signal: The story has no fork in the trail
decision_table.choose: Name the alternative you rejected (package vs thin freeze, Apex vs Flow)
decision_table.not: Say there were no other options
decision_table.why: Trade-offs prove judgment; Well-Architected gives vocabulary

decision_table.choose: Add what you would pack differently next time
decision_table.why: Lessons are changes in your practice, not postcards

decision_table.signal: Resume says 'led CLM' but you configured one field
decision_table.choose: Rewrite the resume line and the deep-dive together
decision_table.not: Keep the inflated line and hope they do not deep-dive

limitations: You cannot always share client metrics; use ranges or LAB_ labels per NDA.
V2MOM wording is optional, not an interview requirement.
Playground projects are valid if labeled as such.
security_notes: Do not paste customer report screenshots with real names into a public portfolio.
NDA-safe deep-dives still tell the truth about ownership.
Do not claim security outcomes you did not test.

troubleshooting.symptom: Interviewer asks 'what did you personally do?' twice

check: Offer how you would measure now

production_notes: Keep a private project log while you work so deep-dives are not reconstructed years later.
Update the resume when ownership changes.

interview_questions.question: How do you structure a Salesforce project deep-dive?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Context, honest ownership, decisions, metrics, lessons, and trade-offs. I shrink to a slice I can defend and I will not invent numbers.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I match a resume line. I spend one minute on the map, two on my pack versus the team's, two on forks, one on a sourced metric or unknown, one on a lesson, one on a trade-off. I practice it. I use Well-Architected only when it names a real choice.
interview_questions.example: Legal-freeze MVP: validation plus UAT owned by me; callout owned by a developer; reversals 6→0 from a report.

interview_questions.question: What is honest ownership in a deep-dive?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I say what I configured or coded, what others did, and what a vendor did. Trailhead says be accurate and do not lie.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Interviewers ask 'what did you personally do?' I pre-answer with I/we/they. In consulting I name the client as org owner. I would rather look smaller and true than large and unverifiable. That protects CAREER-009.
interview_questions.example: I built the rule and the report; Maya wrote the queueable; Acme owned production.
follow_ups: What if you were the only admin?
What if you do not remember?

interview_questions.question: They ask for metrics and you never measured dollars. Answer.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I do not invent savings. I cite a report I have or I say unknown and how I would measure now.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I offer reversals, cycle time, or UAT pass rate if sourced. I do not borrow industry 30% stats. If NDA blocks the number, I give a range or qualitative with permission framing. Accuracy beats a impressive lie.
interview_questions.example: Unknown dollar savings; known: six reversed Closed Won to zero over two quarters, same report.
follow_ups: Can you show a screenshot later?

interview_questions.question: Give a trade-off from a legal-freeze project.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: We chose a thin validation freeze we could maintain instead of buying a legal package this quarter—Easy/readable versus product surface, Trusted sharing via a private child.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I name the alternative: AppExchange legal hold. Cost, licenses, extra automation were the why-not. Risk: we might outgrow the thin freeze. Lesson: revisit if review cycles multiply. I do not smear packages; I say when I would reverse.

interview_questions.question: You started telling a three-year program and they look lost. Recover.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I stop, shrink to one slice with a start and end, and restart ownership.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I say 'let me pick the freeze MVP I actually owned.' I throw away the CLM timeline. I spend the remaining minutes on packs, one metric, one lesson. Deep-dives are not program documentaries.
interview_questions.example: Restart clock: eight weeks, Opportunity freeze, my validation, their callout.
follow_ups: Which slice if you have three?

interview_questions.question: They catch a mismatch with your resume. Recover.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I correct the record immediately, shrink the claim, and offer the true slice.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I do not defend the inflated bullet. Trailhead forbids lying. I say the resume should read configured, not led, and I tell the real ownership. Then I continue the deep-dive on the true work. CAREER-009 is the follow-on discipline.
interview_questions.example: Resume said led CLM; spoken correction: configured freeze MVP.
tradeoffs: Whether to email an updated resume
follow_ups: Do you fix the resume tonight?
weak_answer_warnings: Blaming a recruiter for the bullet and keeping it

interview_questions.question: How do you choose which project to deep-dive for this posting?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I pick the slice whose skills match the posting and whose ownership I can prove, not the flashiest program.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Resume strategies say match the job description. A Flow-heavy posting gets a Flow slice even if I also have a tiny LWC. An architect posting gets sharing trade-offs. I will not pick a story that forces me to invent Apex I did not write.
interview_questions.example: App Builder posting: validation plus Flow; PD posting: the callout you actually wrote, or you say you did not write it and pick another slice.

interview_questions.question: Teach the after-action-report analogy and where it breaks.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Map, packs, GPS, forks, next-time packing. It breaks when you have no GPS—you still do not draw fake elevation.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Context is the map, ownership is packs, metrics are GPS, trade-offs are passes skipped, lessons are packing lists. Postcards are adjective success. It breaks for NDA, for consulting client-owned packs, and because this is not a military product. I then give a 60-second legal-freeze AAR with a sourced metric or unknown.
interview_questions.example: Packs: I = rule+UAT; they = callout. GPS: reversals report. Pass skipped: legal package.
